conclusion.label: endorses

report:
## Conclusion

**Yes—on balance, offering HIV self-testing (HIVST) in addition to standard HIV testing services causes more people to test for HIV.** The strongest evidence comes from systematic reviews of randomized controlled trials, which are well suited to assessing causation.

A 2021 systematic review and meta-analysis of 14 randomized trials (mostly in sub-Saharan Africa) found that HIVST **doubled HIV-testing uptake** in the general population compared with standard services. Effects occurred across several delivery approaches and levels of support, suggesting that the benefit is not limited to one implementation model.  
https://www.thelancet.com/journals/eclinm/article/PIIS2589-5370(21)00271-6/fulltext

This conclusion is consistent with an earlier systematic review/meta-analysis that judged evidence for increased uptake to be of **moderate quality**.  
https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.7448/IAS.20.1.21594

The evidence has informed WHO policy: WHO recommends HIVST as a safe, accurate, effective option to reach people who might otherwise not test—especially key populations, men, and young people.  
https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/WHO-CDS-HIV-19.36

## Important qualification

More testing is not the same as completing HIV care. Some evidence from African studies found lower linkage to care/antiretroviral treatment after self-testing than after conventional services. Thus, an additional self-test offer should include clear confirmatory-testing and care-linkage routes, particularly after a reactive result.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33503050/
